The present petition is an eviction petition filed under Section 14 (1)(e) of DRC Act, whereby the petitioner is seeking eviction of the tenant on the ground of bonafide need.

Hence, before proceedings to appreciate the contentions of the contesting parties in the light of evidence lead during the trial, it is appropriate to reproduce the bare provision of Section 14 (1)(e) of DRC Act.

It reads as under;-
"14. Protection of tenant against eviction, - (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made by and court or Controller in favor of the landlord against a tenant:
Provided that the Controller may, on an application made to him in the prescribed manner, make an order for the recovery of possession of the premises on one or more of the following grounds only, namely:-
(a) ***

8 (b)***
(c)***
(d)***
(e) That the premises are required bona fide by the landlord for himself or for any member of his family dependent on him, if he is the owner thereof, or for any person for whose benefit the premises are held and the landlord or such person has no other reasonably suitable accommodation;
Explanation.-

For the purpose of this clause, "premises let for residential purpose" include any premises which having been let for use as a residence are, without the consent of the landlord, used incidentally for commercial or other purposes;"
22.

In order to establish the grounds for eviction of the tenant/respondent under section 14(1)(e) of the DRC Act, the petitioner must establish the following essentials, viz.
i) Landlord - tenant relationship between the parties; and ii) Petitioner requires the premises bonafide for himself, or for any member of his family dependent upon him; and iii) That the petitioner does not have any other reasonable alternate suitable accommodation.
23. For appropriate adjudication, I shall proceed to critically analyze each of the aforesaid three ingredients/requirements individually.
Landlord-tenant relationship 24.
The respondent herein has not disputed the landlord- tenant relationship between the parties.
Accordingly, the first requirement stands satisfied.
Bonafide requirement 25.
At this juncture, it is necessary to understand what exactly is meant by a 'bonafide' requirement.
26. The phrase 'required bonafide' is suggestive of legislative intent that a mere desire which is outcome of whims or fancy is not taken note of by the rent control legislation.

A requirement in the sense of felt need which is an outcome of a sincere, honest desire, in contradistinction with a mere pretense or pretext to evict a tenant, on the part of the landlord claiming to occupy the premises for himself or for any member of the family would entitle him to seek ejectment of the tenant.

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116669702/
9 27.

The question to be asked for deciding the bonafide by a judge of facts, is by placing himself in the place of the landlord, is, whether in the given facts proved by the material on record the need to occupy the premises can be said to be natural, real, sincere, honest.
If the answer is in positive, the need is bonafide.
The concept of bonafide need or genuine requirement needs a practical approach instructed by the realities of life.

28. The Court would permit the landlord to satisfy the proven need by choosing the accommodation which the landlord feels would be most suited for the purpose; the court would not in such a case thrust its own wisdom upon the choice of the landlord by holding that not one but the other accommodation must be accepted by the landlord to satisfy his need.
29. The full bench of Hon'ble High Court of Madhya Pradesh distinguished between the genuine requirement and the reasonable requirement.

It was held in case of Damodar Sharma & Anr. Vs.
Nandram Deviram that:
"It is wrong to say that "genuinely requires" is the same as "reasonably requires."

sentences.text: There is distinction between the two phrases.
The former phrase refers to a state of mind; the later to an objective standard.
"Genuine requirement" would vary according to the idiosyncrasy of the individual and the time and circumstances in which he lives and thinks.
Reasonable requirement belong to the "knowledge of the law" and means reasonable not in the mind of the person requiring the accommodation but reasonable according to the actual facts.
In my opinion, in this part of section 4(g), the landlord is made the sole arbiter of his own requirements but he must prove that he, in fact, wants and genuinely intends to occupy the premises.

His claim would no doubt fall if the court came to the conclusion that the evidence of "want" was unreliable and that the landlord did not genuinely intend to occupy."
30.

In the matter at hand, the need projected by the petitioner is that the father of the petitioner requires the tenanted premises in question as storage space for his already existing stationary business.

It has been averred by the petitioners that the father of the petitioner is occupying a portion of the residential premises, at the first floor, to satisfy the existing need, however, the same is creating an undue hardship for the other family member.

31. Whereas the respondents have not denied that the father of the petitioner is already engaged in stationary business, it is disputed that he has any further requirement i.e. the tenanted premises in question is needed for additional storage.
It is the argument of the respondents that a stationary business is not something which requires a godown in the background.

Especially considering the fact that the petitioner's father is a retailer, as per the respondents, the additional storage is unwarranted and the same is being fictionally pleaded, only to get the tenanted premises in question vacated.
As per the respondents over the years, the business of father of the petitioner has not seen any exponential growth and therefore the projected requirement is sham.

34. Having heard the submissions and having perused the record, I am of the considered opinion that the requirement projected by the petitioner is bonafide.

By way of evidence on record i.e. the evidence of PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 and the corresponding documents, the petitioners have successfully demonstrated before the court, on the scale of preponderance of probability, that a portion of the suit property which otherwise is in residential occupation of the petitioner is being used for storage of goods of the stationary business of the father of the petitioner.
It is for the storage of these articles, the tenanted premises in question is sought, as additional space.

35. The arguments put forth by the respondent that there is no increase in the income of the petitioner and therefore, it cannot be said that there is expansion or increase in business, is not meritorious as per the Court.
Merely because a business is not generating increased exponential income does not mean that the owner/proprietor of the business cannot seek its expansion.
Seeking expansion of a business is the natural desire of any businessman.
Often expansion is preceded by increased revenue flow, at the same time vice versa is also true i.e. expansion of the business needs to increased flow of revenue.
Both are correct and it is for the owner and the occupier of the business to judge which is more suited to him.
However, it is not for the tenant/respondent to dictate terms nor this court, being Rent Controller, can guide the petitioners on how to run their business.
It is not for the tenant to question the prudence or business acumen of the petitioner.
The argument that there has no expansion in the past is of no value as the absence of expansion in the past does not curtail the right of expansion in the future.

36. In the considered opinion of this Court, the respondents failed to point any material inconsistencies etc. in the course of the cross-examination of the petitioner's witnesses and therefore this Court is of the opinion that the petitioner has successfully pleaded that the need projected by him is bonafide.

The concept of bonafide need or genuine requirement needs a practical approach instructed by the realities of life.

PW-3. Meaning thereby the said shop is not available for the petitioners to take over and utilize for the projected need.
Time and again, the Hon'ble Higher Courts have guided that the requirement of the petitioner must be judged with practical approach.
The aforesaid family settlement was reached at in the course of judicial proceedings, before the Hon'ble High Court.

The same gets also proved,
on the scale of preponderance of probabilities, by the testimony of the petitioner's witnesses.
There is no reason why the court should doubt the bonafide of the said family settlement.

Be that as it may be, the present situation remains that the shop which is projected by the respondent as suitable alternate accommodation is under the occupation of PW-3 and thus, it can be said that the same is not available to the petitioners.
41. A question which arises here is whether the respondent/tenant can dictate which property should be used by the landlord/petitioner.
The answer is a resounding NO.

In plethora of judgments, it has been held time and again that it is not for the tenant to dictate term and the landlord is absolutely free to enjoy the fruit of the property without being guided by the tenant.

42. In the matter at hand as well, since the aforesaid property i.e. the alternate suggested by the respondent (which is shown in yellow colour in the site plan and admitted to be in possession of PW- 3) is already in use and occupation, it cannot be called a suitable alternate accommodation.
In Jagdish Chand Gulati VS. Kanta Devi, 1996 (36) DRJ 654, it was held that the court has to take into consideration the facts which exist at the time of passing of the judgment.

sentences.text: The court finds no force in the argument that the petitioner should get the shop vacated from PW-3 Nitin instead of pressing the present eviction petition.
It is not for the tenant to guide the landlord or dictate terms.

It is trite law that the court would permit the landlord to satisfy the proven need by choosing the accommodation which the landlord feels would be most suited for the purpose; the court would not in such a case thrust its own wisdom upon the choice of the landlord by holding that not one but the other accommodation must be accepted by the landlord to satisfy his need.
Therefore, it can be said that even the third requirement i.e. non- availability of alternate accommodation has been duly proved by the petitioners on the scales of preponderance of probabilities.
44. The fact that the respondent is in occupation of the tenanted premises in question since long is of no consideration.
It is clear that once the landlord establishes its bonafides, the hardship of the tenant cannot be taken into consideration for declining an eviction.

If it is accepted that tenancy should be protected either on the ground of long residency or because of non-availability of house with the tenant, no landlord will ever be able to get an eviction order.
Even otherwise, the law contemplates a buffer period of 6 months for the tenant in which he can arrange for a shelter.
45. Lastly, the arguments raised by the respondent that the father of the petitioners is not dependent upon the petitioners needs to be dealt.
It is trite law that even adult family members can be dependent on the landlord.
It is reasonable to consider the word 'himself' appearing in Section 14(1)(e) of the Act to include the family of the landlord also.
It would be making it completely unworkable if one has to restrict it in grammatical sense.
The word 'himself' cannot necessarily exclude adult and earning members of the family of the landlord or landlady even if they are independent.

Reference is made to the judgment in J.L. Mehta Vs. Smt. Hira Devi, 1970 DLT 484 =
1971 RCJ 272.
46.

sentences.text: To conclude this discussion, it can be said that the petitioner in the eviction petition, in clear and unequivocal terms has mentioned about his requirements.
It is not only the "mere desire" of the petitioner to get the premises vacated but it needs the same for above stated requirements.
The pleas made by the respondent are sans merits.
47. In view of all the above findings, the present eviction petition is allowed.

Hence, an eviction order is passed against the respondent in respect of the tenanted premises i.e. one shop on the ground floor, forming part of the property bearing No.223, Gali No.9, Padam Nagar, Kishan Ganj,
Delhi-110007, as specifically shown in the red colour in the plan attached with the petition.

48. The petitioner, however, would not be entitled to obtain possession of the tenanted premises before the expiration of a period of six months from the date of this order in terms of section 14(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
